newsitem.title: ITALY: Top managers call for early Stet sale.
newsitem.headline: Top managers call for early Stet sale.

text.p: Top Italian state managers called on Thursday for state telecoms group Stet to be sold as soon as possible to stave off the bankruptcy of its parent company -- state holding IRI.
"If IRI does not sell Stet and its other activities, serious damage is in store for the public purse," said IRI chairman Michele Tedeschi in an interview with Turin daily La Stampa.

Stet's Managing Director Ernesto Pascale also added his voice to those seeking an early sale of IRI's dominant stake in the telecoms group and said that the government should bring forward a deadline of March 31, 1997.
"The sooner it is done the better," Pascale told left-wing Rome daily in an interview. "If I could chose I would say Febuary 1, 1997 rather than March 31," he added.
Pascale said the company was suffering as a result of the uncertainty as to when it would be sold to private investors. "You cannot work well in a climate of continuous debate," he said.

The sale of Stet, which controls Italy's main fixed line and mobile phone operators, ran into trouble on Tuesday when a parliamentary commission abandoned work on a watchdog body for the sector because of political filibustering.
The Treasury said on Wednesday it hoped Stet would be sold by the current deadline, so it can take advantage of a window of opportunity in Europe's busy privatisation programme.
"If this is not possible...the Stet sale will still go ahead in 1997, as soon as the watchdog authority is approved," the Treasury statement said.
Italy has promised the European Union it will sell the huge telecoms group by next June, as part of a 1993 deal.
Under the accord, IRI must cut its debt to below five trillion lire ($3.3 billion) by the end of 1996. At the end of 1995 its net debt stood at 22.456 trillion lire.

Prime minister Romano Prodi is reported to be convinced that an early Stet sale offers the best chance of heading off a full-blown crisis at IRI which is expected to lose more than three trillion lire in 1996.
IRI owns a clutch of companies in addition to Stet, including state carrier Alitalia, engineering group Finmeccanica and shipbuilding company Fincantieri.
If IRI's 1996 losses are in line with forecasts, half the group's equity base would be wiped out, forcing the company to sell assets or seek a cash injection.

Prodi, who spent two stints at the head of IRI in the 1980s and early 1990s, is reported to firmly oppose a Treasury proposal to plug the hole in IRI's balance sheet by transferring to IRI a company called Gepi. He has also dismissed another Treasury idea of hiving off IRI's debts together with its most sellable assets into a separate company.

One of the factors delaying the Stet sale was the government's inability until now to put together a "hard core" of shareholders along the French model who would ensure a stable ownership of the telecoms group after it is privatised.
"The government is weak and it is not able to create this hard core of shareholders," said a prominent expert on Italian state industry, who asked not to be named.

Unlike countries such as Britain, where institutional investors have channelled savings into privatised companies, pension funds and unit trusts (mutual funds) are still relatively undeveloped in Italy.

Some politicians fear that a Stet in private hands would quickly be drawn into the orbit of the country's biggest industrial group, Fiat, and its powerful banking ally, Mediobanca. ($ = 1514 Italian Lire)
